pitfalls: Suspicion time is vague → use the first note mentioning cord compression.
Out-of-hours radiography staffing → agree cover with radiology before the change.
Referrals come from many teams → use the coordinator log as the single source.
Scans at other sites → include transfer times.
pearls: Recruit the acute oncology lead and MSCC coordinator.
Record dexamethasone as a secondary measure; it is often missed.
Report by hour of referral; night referrals show the gap.

pitfalls: Repatriated patients get letters from the local hospital → audit the neurosurgical transfer letter.
Plan decided later at MDT → allow 'to be confirmed by letter by date X' with a contact.
Template fields ignored → make them mandatory in the e-discharge system.
Small numbers → use 6 months.
pearls: Recruit the SAH or vascular nurse specialist.
Prefill the contact to save junior time.
Include paper copy given as a secondary measure.

pitfalls: Pre-operative statin simply continued → count continuation of a lower dose without reason as a fail.
Interactions (e.g. with some antiarrhythmics) → accept documented pharmacist advice.
Surgeons defer to cardiologists → agree the default with both before cycle 1.
Reason boxes filled with 'n/a' → spot-check reasons.
pearls: Recruit the cardiac surgical pharmacist.
Pull prescriptions from the e-discharge system in bulk.
Feed back to the cardiac rehab team to reinforce.

pitfalls: Epicardial pacing or inotropes make many ineligible → record contraindications and report the eligible denominator.
Medicines reconciliation incomplete → confirm pre-operative use from the GP summary care record.
ICU and ward teams hand over poorly → put the default in the ICU order set so it travels.
Postoperative AF numbers are small → treat as descriptive.
pearls: Recruit a cardiac intensivist and the ICU pharmacist.
Agree the haemodynamic thresholds before cycle 1.
Show AF rates by restart status.

pitfalls: Patients from other regions need referral to distant services → keep a regional service list in the template.
Rehabilitation teams refer later from clinic → record any later referral separately.
Opt-out referrals rejected for incomplete data → include minimum dataset fields.
Extending to all CABG changes the denominator → keep the MI group for the re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the cardiac rehabilitation lead nurse.
Check the NACR submission for the same patients.
Measure uptake (first session attended) later as an outcome.

pitfalls: Nodes sent together as one pot cannot be mapped → the labelled pots fix this.
Wedge resections in frail patients → report by resection type.
Pathology reports use different station labels → agree IASLC station names with pathology.
Surgeons see the pass bar as low → add station 7 and ≥3 N2 stations as secondary measures.
pearls: Recruit a thoracic pathologist as co-lead.
Keep the pass criterion simple in cycle 1; add ESTS detail later.
Report upstaging (N1/N2 found) to show benefit.

pitfalls: Surgeons worry about thrombosis in cancer or vascular patients → agree a short contraindication list with haematology before cycle 1 and count a documented reason as a pass.
Tranexamic acid given at closure is recorded but not at induction → record the time and report timing separately from 'given at all'.
Minor procedures swamp the sample → define 'risk of bleeding' locally (e.g. any procedure with a group and save) and keep the same definition in both cycles.
Default chart line ignored by locums → add it to the Sign In so the ODP asks every case.
pearls: Recruit the transfusion practitioner; the 2026 NICE update is on their audit list.
Pull cases from the theatre system by specialty so one audit covers several teams.
Ask pharmacy to stock 1 g tranexamic acid in every anaesthetic room drug drawer.
Name a consultant anaesthetist lead who will keep the chart default after the trainee rotates.

pitfalls: Eating status not recorded → accept any documented oral medicine given at the same time as proof oral route was possible.
Anaesthetists prescribe IV paracetamol in recovery 'regular' → agree with the anaesthetic department that PACU prescriptions are 'once only' or 24 hours.
Nurses give IV because it is quicker on rounds → involve ward sisters in the change.
Pharmacy switch not sustained after rotation → put the rule in EPMA, not in teaching.
pearls: Ask pharmacy for an EPMA report of IV paracetamol by ward; it takes minutes.
Show the cost difference per dose at the first presentation.
Recruit a ward pharmacist as co-lead.
Lock the 'cannot take oral' definition before cycle 1.

pitfalls: Monitor records temperature but it is not exported to the chart → check that the data feed is on before cycle 1.
Tympanic infrared readings are indirect estimates (NICE 1.1.6) → record the site and report it separately.
Short cases with one reading distort results → apply the >30-minute rule in both cycles.
Staff see it as box-ticking → show the recovery hypothermia rate alongside compliance.
pearls: Recruit an ODP lead; ODPs usually place the probe.
Audit one theatre suite first if paper charts are mixed with electronic ones.
Record the lowest temperature too; it makes the case for warming equipment.
Ask the theatre educator to add the probe to the room set-up checklist.

pitfalls: Departure time not recorded → use the theatre 'patient arrived in reception' time minus porter time, and keep the same rule in both cycles.
Ward nurses object to extra observations → the field replaces a free-text line on the existing checklist.
Emergency patients sent urgently → accept 'clinical urgency' documented as an exclusion.
Gains fade after rotation → make the field mandatory in the electronic checklist.
pearls: Recruit a ward sister and a theatre reception nurse.
Theatre reception can refuse to accept a checklist without the temperature during weeks 5–12.
Report how many patients were below 36.0°C; it shows why it matters.
Agree the time source before cycle 1.

pitfalls: Nurses feel blamed by incident reporting → frame reports as capacity data for the board, not individual error.
Decision time and actual time confused → record both; the standard is about actual transfer.
Small numbers → use all discharges over 3 months, not a sample.
Bed managers push back → invite them to the presentation and show readmission data.
pearls: ICNARC case mix data already hold discharge times; ask the ICNARC data clerk.
Recruit the ICU matron as co-lead.
Report time from decision to discharge; it shows the day-time delays that cause night moves.
Keep the report monthly after the audit.

pitfalls: Night calls happen by phone and are not written → a timed name field fixes documentation, not behaviour; audit out-of-hours separately.
Parent consultants feel policed → present as shared decision-making support, with parent-team representation.
Referral through outreach blurs who spoke to whom → record the parent consultant contact explicitly.
Definitions drift → lock the exclusion list before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit an acute medicine consultant; most ward admissions are medical.
Check that the ICU admission proforma is the source of truth before cycle 1.
Report the proportion with a treatment escalation plan at the same time; it is often the real gap.
Name an ICU consultant sponsor.

pitfalls: Physiotherapists record goals in a separate system → agree before cycle 1 which records count.
Sedated patients cannot agree goals → count family involvement or documented reason, as NICE allows.
At-risk definition changes between cycles → write the criteria on the data sheet.
Weekend admissions missed → report weekday and weekend admissions separately.
pearls: Recruit the lead ICU physiotherapist as co-lead.
Use the NCEPOD 2025 audit toolkit fields where they match.
Present with a patient story from the follow-up clinic.
Add the box to the day-3 ward round so it is part of routine care.

pitfalls: Handover is verbal between physiotherapists → count only written handover and say so.
Summary written by a junior doctor without therapy input → build the section so the physiotherapist can complete it.
Night discharges skip the summary → cross-check with audit 'night discharges'.
Section filled with 'see physio notes' → define what counts as a plan.
pearls: Recruit ICU and ward physiotherapists together.
Check 48-hour ward therapy review as an outcome; it shows impact.
Use the same at-risk list as the rehabilitation-goals audit.
Ask the EPR team for a template change early; it can take weeks.

pitfalls: No follow-up clinic exists → first measure referrals and present the gap to the business planning meeting.
Outcome lags by 3 months → audit referral rate at re-audit and attendance later.
Patients die or move after discharge → exclude and report them separately.
Clinic capacity fills → agree nurse-led or virtual review models with the ICU lead.
pearls: Recruit the ICU follow-up nurse or the lead physiotherapist.
Ask ICUsteps or the patient group for a patient voice at the presentation.
The NCEPOD 2025 audit toolkit fits this audit.
Separate 'not offered' from 'did not attend'.

pitfalls: ICU summary written in jargon → pair the change with a lay-language section.
Ward nurses do not know the patient was in ICU → use an EPR trigger.
Giving a copy is not documented even when done → the checklist tick fixes this.
Low numbers per ward → sample hospital-wide.
pearls: Recruit the ICU follow-up nurse.
Check GP receipt at the same time; it is often missing.
Ask a former patient to review the summary wording.
Keep the checklist item after the audit.

pitfalls: Clinic time is short → standing BP adds 3 minutes; show the falls risk data.
Telephone pre-assessments cannot measure it → exclude them and report the proportion.
Drops found but not acted on → add a 'drop found: action' field.
Automated cuffs give wrong readings on standing → agree a method (1 and 3 minutes) before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the pre-assessment nurse lead.
Ask the falls team to support the presentation.
Report the number of significant drops found; it motivates staff.
Use the same eligibility list in both cycles.

pitfalls: Some anaesthetists still prefer to omit → share the guideline and allow a documented individual decision.
Old leaflets remain in circulation → recall and replace all printed stock.
Whether the dose was taken is not recorded → add it to the admission checklist.
Hypotension after induction worries staff → record pre-induction BP and report it.
pearls: Recruit a pre-assessment pharmacist.
Check all instruction sources (leaflet, letter, electronic list) before cycle 1.
Present the national guideline change as the reason, not local opinion.
Name a consultant owner for the medication instruction sheet.

pitfalls: Reason codes are vague ('medical') → search the anaesthetic notes for BP values.
Anxiety readings on the day → require repeated readings and record them.
Anaesthetists feel second-guessed → present as a department standard agreed at a meeting.
Low monthly numbers → use 12 months for cycle 1 and 6 months for cycle 2.
pearls: Recruit the theatre manager; cancellation data are theirs.
Present minutes of theatre time lost.
Ask pre-assessment to request GP readings for anyone at 160/100 or above.
Name a consultant for the second-opinion rule.

pitfalls: Weight-loss injections bought privately are missing from GP lists → ask directly at pre-assessment.
Staff still stop the drug for a week → record 'stopped' separately and share the new guidance.
Definitions of 'assessment' vary → agree minimum content before cycle 1.
Few cases in cycle 1 → extend the time window, not the inclusion criteria.
pearls: Recruit a pre-assessment pharmacist to search medication lists.
Include endoscopy sedation lists; they see many of these patients.
Share the national consensus infographic with the change.
Name a consultant who owns the local guide.

pitfalls: Heart failure patients are not flagged as 'diabetic' → search by drug name, not diagnosis.
Only day-of omission advised → check the wording of every leaflet.
Whether the day-before dose was taken is not asked → add it to the admission checklist.
Cardiologists worry about stopping → the omission is only 2 days; share the consensus.
pearls: Recruit a pharmacist to run a drug-name search.
Include day-surgery units.
Add restart advice at discharge in the same change.
Keep the drug list up to date as new SGLT2 inhibitors appear.

pitfalls: Meter readings are not transcribed → download from the meter to check.
Short cases under an hour → need only one intra-operative reading; define rules before cycle 1.
Recovery nurses unaware of VRII → include recovery staff in the change.
Few eligible patients → extend the time window.
pearls: Recruit the inpatient diabetes specialist nurse.
Ask point-of-care testing for meter data by location.
Report hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia episodes as outcomes.
Use the same gap rule in both cycles.

pitfalls: Dexamethasone avoided in diabetes → record the reason; a documented alternative counts.
Apfel score not documented → derive it from the notes and keep the same method in both cycles.
Anaesthetists resist 'recipe' anaesthesia → keep an untick-with-reason option.
PONV outcome under-recorded in recovery → add a yes/no field to the recovery chart.
pearls: Recruit the recovery sister to record PONV and rescue.
Present day-case unplanned admissions due to PONV if available.
Pharmacy can confirm drug stock in each anaesthetic room.
Run cycle 1 on the same lists you will re-audit.

pitfalls: Recovery nurses only have ondansetron under a PGD → update the PGD or order set before cycle 2.
Prophylaxis not recorded clearly → use the electronic chart as the only source.
Droperidol availability varies → offer two alternatives in the ladder.
Ward and recovery rescue differ → report both settings separately.
pearls: Recruit a recovery nurse and a surgical pharmacist.
Collect second-rescue rates; they show the benefit.
Show the ladder on the recovery drug trolley.
Pair this audit with the prophylaxis audit for one presentation.

pitfalls: Capnography used but not written down → the checklist line fixes documentation; say so when presenting.
Cardiac arrest forms lack the field → update the resuscitation record too.
Low trace in cardiac arrest confuses staff → include the PUMA 'sustained CO2' criteria on the checklist.
Small numbers per month → collect from ICU, ED and arrest calls together.
pearls: Recruit an ICU airway lead and an ED consultant.
Check every emergency airway trolley has a working capnography line during weeks 5–12.
Record videolaryngoscope use at the same time.
Report any recognised oesophageal intubations anonymously.

pitfalls: Low volume → use 6–12 months for cycle 1 and keep collecting until 20 cases for cycle 2.
Obs recorded but no wound check → the field must be separate.
Patients moved to wards far from the nursing station → record bed location too.
Night staffing pushback → hourly obs apply only to the first 6 hours.
pearls: Recruit the ENT or endocrine ward sister.
Check for the post-thyroid emergency box at the same time.
Invite the thyroid surgeon to co-present.
Use the DAS/BAETS/ENT UK post-thyroid surgery review chart as the template.

pitfalls: BMI missing for emergency cases → allow 'estimated' and record weight on admission.
Patients object to BMI on public screens → show a neutral flag icon rather than the number.
Booking clerks bypass mandatory fields → ask IT to block list publication without BMI.
Definitions change (BMI >35 vs >40) → keep 40 in both cycles.
pearls: Recruit the theatre scheduling manager.
Check emergency lists separately; they fail most.
Show a near miss (equipment not ready) to explain why.
Record team brief discussion as a second measure.

pitfalls: Theatre lines documented on the anaesthetic chart only → accept the chart if the witness is named.
Assistants not trained to witness → brief ODPs and ICU nurses before the change.
Paper stickers run out → keep stock in every line trolley and add an EPR version.
Emergency lines out of hours are missed → audit day and night separately.
pearls: Recruit the ICU nurse educator and the theatre ODP lead.
Record ultrasound use too; it is in the same guideline.
Keep a blank form on the CVC trolley.
Present any Never Event learning nationally to show relevance.

pitfalls: Surgeons and anaesthetists each assume the other consents → agree who owns it before cycle 1.
Consent recorded only when transfusion happens → sample from the cross-match list, not the transfusion list.
Jehovah's Witness patients distort results → include them; an advance decision counts as a documented discussion.
Section left blank on the form → make it mandatory for listed procedures.
pearls: Recruit the transfusion practitioner.
Use the NHS Blood and Transplant patient leaflet.
Link the change to the maximum surgical blood ordering schedule.
Report alternatives offered; it supports patient blood management.

pitfalls: CPAP use not asked at pre-assessment → add a yes/no question first.
Patients forget despite instruction → add a text reminder the day before.
Wards lack power points or staff familiar with CPAP → involve the respiratory nurse.
Small numbers → extend the collection window.
pearls: Recruit the sleep or respiratory physiology team.
Include day-surgery units.
Record post-op CPAP use as an outcome.
Keep the same inclusion in both cycles.

pitfalls: Time zero recorded differently between cycles → agree in advance that time zero is the first ED NEWS2 time stamp, not triage or doctor review.
Prescription time used instead of administration time → take only the 'given' time from EPMA.
Medium-risk patients with a 3-point single parameter caused by infection are missed → add a column and decide inclusion rules before cycle 1.
Nursing staff see the audit as blame → share results by shift pattern, not by name.
Gains fade after rotation → make the alert part of the system, not a poster.
pearls: Recruit the ED sepsis nurse and the EPR analyst on day 1; they can pull NEWS2 time stamps in bulk.
Record the reason for each delay; the commonest cause tells you which fix to pick.
Use a run chart of weekly compliance, not a single percentage.
Hand the monthly report to a consultant owner before you rotate.

pitfalls: Old 500 ml bags or stickers left in resus → remove old stock labels and stickers on the change date.
Paramedic pre-alert fluids counted as the first bolus → record pre-hospital fluid separately.
Clinicians object that 250 ml is too little in shock → share the NG253 wording and stress repeat boluses up to 1,000 ml.
Reassessment not written down → accept a timed set of observations as reassessment.
pearls: Agree definitions with the ED sepsis lead before cycle 1.
Ask pharmacy to change the order set default; it is quick and lasts beyond rotation.
Pair the audit with the antibiotic timing audit to share data collection.
Report total fluid in the first hour too, to show no one is under-resuscitated.

pitfalls: Grade of reviewer not recorded → use the rota or login name to confirm grade.
Lactate done on the arterial gas instead → accept any blood gas lactate.
Patients escalate to high risk and drop out → record them and analyse separately.
Night-time staffing skews results → report by time of day.
pearls: Get the ED nurse in charge to agree triage-led venous gas before cycle 1.
Pull NEWS2 5–6 plus infection codes from the EPR to find cases fast.
Record the antibiotic decision to show safe deferral, not just speed.
Present results with the high-risk antibiotic audit as one sepsis story.

pitfalls: Small numbers in a DGH → extend the look-back to 6 months or share with a neighbouring ED.
Criterion time hard to find → use the first PEWS chart entry showing the criterion.
Cannulation delays blamed → record access method and attempts.
Paediatric and ED teams dispute ownership → run it as a joint audit with named leads from each.
pearls: Recruit a paediatric nurse champion to check the grab box daily.
Use the ED coding for 'sepsis' and 'fever' to find cases.
Agree what counts as the criterion time before cycle 1.
Give weight-band dosing cards to reduce prescribing delay.

pitfalls: Triage staff resist more mandatory fields → agree with the nurse lead and show baseline data first.
CRT entered as '<2' by default → check for copy-forward values.
Only initial observations audited → keep to first assessment to avoid mixed definitions.
Streamed children seen in UTC are missed → include UTC or state exclusion.
pearls: Recruit a paediatric ED nurse to co-lead.
Collect traffic light category too; it adds value at no extra time.
Show missing CRT by time of day to target training.
A mandatory field keeps working after rotation.

pitfalls: Risk factor time is not written → use the first note describing it and record how often it is missing.
Radiology feels blamed → run it jointly with a radiology lead.
Request made late, not scan late → record request time to split ED and radiology delay.
Changing inclusion between cycles → use the same list of 7 risk factors.
pearls: Get CT acquisition times in bulk from RIS.
Split the timeline into identify → request → scan → report.
Recruit a CT superintendent radiographer early.
Show the worst delays as short case stories at governance.

pitfalls: Patients with other risk factors slip in → screen each case against recs 1.5.8 and 1.5.9 first.
Aspirin alone included by mistake → exclude aspirin monotherapy.
Clinicians fear missing a bleed → present yield and the NICE rationale together.
Injury time missing → record 'unknown' and treat as presenting after 8 hours.
pearls: Pull cases from the ED head injury code plus medication list.
Report the CT yield; it helps the department agree a local stance.
Get a consultant to sign off the proforma wording.
Keep the box short so it gets used.

pitfalls: Injury time not recorded → make it a required field; record 'unknown' in cycle 1.
Children observed in a separate area with paper charts → check both paper and electronic records.
Breach pressure pushes early discharge → share with the site team that observation counts as care.
Multi-factor children included by mistake → screen for 1.5.10 and 1.5.11 factors first.
pearls: Recruit a paediatric ED nurse to check the 'discharge not before' box.
Report deterioration during observation to show why the rule matters.
Use the tracking board so the time is visible to all.
Agree the proforma change with the paediatric lead before cycle 1.

pitfalls: Letters generated but not sent → check the sent log, not the draft.
Health visitor contact unknown → route via the paediatric liaison team.
IT change takes months → start with a manual liaison list while the build is done.
Adults included by mistake → restrict to under 16.
pearls: Recruit the paediatric liaison health visitor as co-lead.
The safeguarding lead will back this; ask early.
Audit copy recipients, not just timing.
Keep a small weekly spot check after the change.

pitfalls: No falls service capacity → agree the referral route with the service before cycle 1.
GP letter wording counted as referral → define what counts before cycle 1.
Patients from care homes already known → record as 'already under falls team'.
Tick box ignored → make it a required field on discharge.
pearls: Recruit the frailty or falls nurse lead early.
Report CFS alongside to show need.
Show the number of repeat attendances with falls to motivate staff.
Keep the referral one click.

pitfalls: Onset time unknown → use the ambulance call time and note it.
Allergic reactions without adrenaline included → restrict to IM adrenaline cases.
Small numbers → use 12 months look-back and report as counts.
Second sample forgotten at handover → put the task on the tracking board.
pearls: Ask the lab to report sample collection time, not receipt time.
Recruit the local allergy consultant; they want this data.
Pair with the auto-injector and referral audit to share case finding.
Build the order set once; it outlasts rotation.

pitfalls: Patients already carrying devices not checked for expiry → add 'in date' to the checkbox.
Out-of-hours pharmacy cannot supply → keep two devices as ED pre-packs.
Drug-trigger exemptions overused → require the drug name.
Training not recorded → accept a nursing note naming the device brand.
pearls: Recruit the ED pharmacist to build the default TTO.
Keep brand-specific trainer pens at the nurse station.
Record allergy referral in the same pass; NG258 rec 1.1.12 asks for it.
Share results with the allergy clinic to secure their support.

pitfalls: Wells written after the test → compare time stamps.
PERC used instead of Wells in low-risk patients → record PERC use as a separate field.
Radiology vetting already enforces it informally → check with radiology to avoid double work.
Required field filled with random numbers → spot check 10 scores for accuracy.
pearls: Report CTPA positive rate; it is the outcome consultants care about.
Recruit a radiology registrar to share data pulls.
Include the age-adjusted D-dimer question as a secondary measure.
Agree the form change with the IT team before cycle 1.

pitfalls: Wells not written → count as fail and report separately.
Ambulatory clinic records live on paper → include both sources.
Clinicians worry about bleeding → include contraindication as a pass route.
Weekend scan availability changes between cycles → record day of week.
pearls: Recruit the anticoagulation nurse specialist as co-lead.
Report time of day; out-of-hours is where it fails.
Check baseline bloods are sent (NG158 1.3.4).
Keep the pre-printed line simple, with a renal dose table on the back.

pitfalls: Liaison psychiatry notes still use ratings → include them and discuss with the mental health trust.
Staff feel the old score protects them → explain the NICE rationale and offer a needs-based alternative.
Template change takes months → start with a paper version.
Hard to judge 'used for decision' → count any rating as fail in both cycles.
pearls: Co-lead with a liaison psychiatry nurse.
Use the RCEM mental health toolkit wording in the new template.
Also record whether liaison referral was offered.
Get the mental health trust to agree the change before cycle 1.

pitfalls: Adolescents seen in the adult ED are missed → search both areas.
CAMHS assessment counted as ED assessment → count only ED clinician notes.
ED doctors lack HEADSSS confidence → add a prompt card with questions.
Data entry doubles with the RCEM portal → use the same fields as the QIP.
pearls: Register with the RCEM QIP to benchmark nationally.
Recruit the paediatric mental health lead nurse.
Record CAMHS response time as a secondary measure.
Share anonymised good examples with the team.

pitfalls: AF with rapid rate admitted → restrict to discharges only.
Known AF on anticoagulant included → exclude.
ED staff say it is the GP's job → the NICE wording covers any setting; share the stroke risk.
Score calculated but wrong → spot check 10 scores.
pearls: Recruit a cardiology or AF nurse specialist.
Record the plan, not just the score.
Include ORBIT as a secondary measure.
Put the calculator in the template, not on a poster.

pitfalls: Advice given verbally but not written → only count written advice in both cycles.
Staff unsure of DVLA rules → include a one-page summary with the template.
Simple vasovagal faints have different rules → record diagnosis so advice can be checked.
Non-drivers counted as fails → record 'does not drive' as pass if asked.
pearls: Pair with a 12-lead ECG check; same notes, extra value.
Recruit an ED consultant with an interest in syncope.
Link the template to the DVLA web page.
A required field keeps working after rotation.

pitfalls: Overdose type not clear in notes → record 'unclear' and treat as unknown time.
Waiting for weight → use weight-band tables.
Pharmacy prescribing delays at night → keep weight-band bags in ED.
Small numbers → extend the look-back.
pearls: Recruit the ED pharmacist.
Check dose accuracy at the same time.
Use TOXBASE wording in the pathway.
Share with liaison psychiatry to align the timing of assessment.

pitfalls: Paper FP10 prescriptions missed → include ED pharmacy TTO records.
Microbiology advice verbal → accept 'discussed with micro' plus reason.
Drop-down filled without thought → spot check 10 against the notes.
Pushback from urology or ENT pathways → agree exemptions with specialty leads.
pearls: Recruit the antimicrobial pharmacist; they can pull a dispensing list in minutes.
Report by indication; UTI and prostatitis dominate.
Print the MHRA patient sheet into the discharge pack.
Share results with the stewardship committee for Trust-wide spread.

pitfalls: Capnography modules missing → check equipment before cycle 1.
Proforma not used → count free-text notes too and report proforma use.
Sedation lead not involved → ask them to co-lead.
Paediatric sedation mixed in → keep to adults or audit separately.
pearls: Ask the ED sedation lead to present the results and own the proforma.
Record adverse events as a balancing measure.
Keep capnography lines with each monitor.
Build it into sedation competency.

pitfalls: Usual dose times not known → ask patient or carer and record at triage.
Self-administered doses not recorded → add a self-administration entry on EPMA.
Short ED stays with no dose due → exclude them.
Pharmacy stock gaps → agree an ED stock list with pharmacy.
pearls: Register with the RCEM QIP to benchmark.
Recruit a Parkinson's nurse specialist.
Use Parkinson's UK 'Get it on time' materials.
Report missed doses as counts; they are powerful at governance.

pitfalls: Dipsticks done by nurses but not written anywhere → agree before cycle 1 where the result is recorded (observations chart or EPR) and search both.
Catheterised or anuric patients skew results → exclude anuric patients and record catheter status as a note.
Small numbers of stage 2–3 AKI → report all stages together and stage 2–3 separately.
The bundle field gets ticked without a real result → count a pass only if analyte values are recorded.
pearls: Recruit the AKI specialist nurse or outreach team; they already review alerts daily.
Ask the ward managers to stock dipsticks and pots at the nurses' station on each medical ward.
Pair the change with a one-line rule on the AKI alert: 'Dip the urine now'.
Hand the dashboard to the renal link nurse so it survives the rotation.

pitfalls: Few cases → extend the retrospective window and consider a regional collaboration.
Antibiotic given but not charted in ED → check the ED drugs record and nursing notes.
Cirrhosis not known at arrival → record whether cirrhosis was known and report both groups.
Order set ignored at night → ask the ED lead to include it in the GI bleed triage card.
pearls: Recruit the hepatology nurse specialist to identify cases.
Use the BSG decompensated cirrhosis bundle as the vehicle, since many trusts already have it.
Agree the antibiotic choice with microbiology first so the order set is unarguable.
Report infection rate alongside compliance.

pitfalls: Previous SBP (secondary prophylaxis) wrongly failed → record it and count it as indicated.
Child–Pugh or MELD not calculable from records → collect raw values and calculate centrally.
Hepatologists disagree with the 2023 change → agree the standard at the MDT before cycle 1.
Stopping prophylaxis worries GPs → include a line in the clinic letter explaining the change.
pearls: Recruit a hepatology pharmacist; they can pull all ciprofloxacin/co-trimoxazole repeat prescriptions for liver patients.
Report fluoroquinolone exposure avoided as a stewardship win.
Run the audit from clinic lists so you can act at the next appointment.
Add a stop date or review date to every prophylaxis prescription.

pitfalls: HAS-BLED still embedded in local templates → replace, do not add, or both get skipped.
Scores done on apps but not written → count only documented scores; say so at teaching.
Clinicians fear ORBIT will deny anticoagulation → stress it guides risk discussion, not a cut-off.
Starts in clinics missed → limit to inpatient starts for cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the anticoagulation pharmacist; they review every new start already.
Put CHA2DS2-VASc and ORBIT side by side on the same form.
Pre-fill ORBIT items from the lab to cut effort.
Ask the cardiology lead to email the change to all medical registrars.

pitfalls: Aspirin started years ago in primary care → count it and give the GP a clear recommendation in the discharge letter.
Other antiplatelet indications missed → check cardiology history and stents before failing a case.
Frail patients' 'no anticoagulant' decisions labelled as fails → record documented decisions separately.
Pharmacist capacity → run the check only for AF discharges flagged by the EPR.
pearls: Recruit a ward pharmacist as co-lead.
Use the EPR problem list to find AF patients quickly.
Give a one-line script for the discharge letter: 'Aspirin stopped; anticoagulation discussed'.
Report strokes avoided using simple CHA2DS2-VASc rates to engage managers.

pitfalls: LVEF missing or old → use the most recent echo within 12 months and record the date.
Drugs held for acute kidney injury never restarted → count a documented 'restart plan' as a reason.
Cardiology and general medicine patients differ → report the two groups separately.
Checklist ticked without reasons → make the reason box mandatory for any 'no'.
pearls: Recruit the heart failure specialist nurses; they hold the NHFA list.
Pre-fill the checklist from the discharge prescription so it takes seconds.
Ask the pharmacist to flag missing SGLT2 inhibitors on the discharge screen.
Add titration instructions for the GP to the same template.

pitfalls: Echo done after discharge → record the date and count only pre-discharge assessment for the first part.
Result in the cath report but not the letter → the pass needs the letter, as the GP relies on it.
Type 2 MI coded as NSTEMI → use MINAP type 1 NSTEMI only.
Mandatory field filled with 'see notes' → define acceptable entries.
pearls: Recruit the MINAP audit clerk to supply cases.
Ask echo to prioritise inpatient ACS scans before discharge.
Auto-pull the latest EF from the echo system into the template if possible.
Report the number of low-EF patients who missed MRA or device review.

pitfalls: Ward has no medical air outlets → check supply with estates first; portable air compressors may be needed.
Nurses choose the gas regardless of prescription → include nursing staff in the teaching and record the gas used where charted.
Blood gas not done → record hypercapnia as unknown and report separately.
IT change delayed → use a chart sticker as an interim fix.
pearls: Recruit a respiratory nurse specialist and the e-prescribing pharmacist early.
Build the default from the prescribed oxygen target range to cut clicks.
Put 'Air-driven nebs' signs by COPD beds.
Share results through the NACAP quarterly report.

pitfalls: Doses given before admission not counted → record GP or ambulance rescue-pack doses.
Asthma overlap cases prescribed longer courses → exclude documented overlap under specialist care.
Discharge letter restarts a fresh 5 days → check the discharge prescription carefully.
Order set bypassed via free text → review free-text steroid prescriptions in cycle 2.
pearls: Recruit the COPD nurse specialist who already runs the discharge bundle.
Print 'Day x of 5' on the drug chart line.
Ask the pharmacist to reconcile steroid days on discharge.
Report cumulative steroid exposure avoided.

pitfalls: Previous-admission gases hard to find → search the blood gas archive by hospital number before cycle 1.
Nurses start Scale 2 from habit → include nursing leads in the change.
Scale 2 carried over between admissions → record whether it was re-confirmed.
IT lock not feasible → use a mandatory note template linked to the Scale 2 option.
pearls: Recruit the outreach team lead; they see missed deteriorations.
Pull the Scale 2 list directly from the e-observations system.
Report any case where Scale 1 would have triggered a higher response.
Give registrars a one-line rule: 'No gas, no Scale 2'.

pitfalls: Discharge supplies add days → always count discharge prescriptions.
IV-to-oral switch restarts the clock → make the counter shared.
Hospital-acquired pneumonia mixed in → confirm onset within 48 hours of admission.
Clinicians fear under-treatment → share the NICE instability criteria as the only reasons to extend.
pearls: Recruit the antimicrobial pharmacist as co-lead.
Report antibiotic days saved per 40 patients.
Add the 5-day rule to the post-take ward round template.
Share results with GPs, as many courses end in the community.

pitfalls: Low case numbers → use a 12-month window or pool with a neighbouring trust.
Genuine PPI indications failed → accept a documented indication (e.g. Barrett's, recent GI bleed).
PPI restarted at discharge → check the discharge prescription.
Infection team and ward team each assume the other acts → name the ward pharmacist as owner.
pearls: Recruit the infection prevention nurse who reviews every case.
Add the PPI question to the existing root-cause analysis form.
Ask the pharmacist to flag PPIs when toxin results come back.
Give GPs a clear stop or review instruction.

pitfalls: 'Unprovoked' labelled inconsistently → define it before cycle 1 (no major transient risk factor in the preceding 3 months).
Imaging requested by GPs later → check order comms for 3 months after diagnosis.
Symptoms documented after the scan → require documentation before the request.
Clinicians worry about missed cancer → report 12-month cancer outcomes alongside.
pearls: Recruit the thrombosis nurse who runs the DVT clinic.
Ask radiology to vet 'occult malignancy' CT requests against the pathway.
Report avoided scans and cost to managers.
Keep the change within the existing clinic proforma.

pitfalls: Score calculated but not written → count only documented scores.
No ambulatory pathway exists → agree follow-up capacity with the ambulatory unit first.
Low-risk patients admitted for social reasons → record the reason.
Small numbers of outpatients → report readmissions carefully with raw numbers.
pearls: Recruit an ambulatory care consultant.
Link the sPESI box to the ambulatory referral in one click.
Give patients the NG158 contact details sheet.
Report bed-days saved to operational managers.

pitfalls: Gout flares poorly coded → find cases through colchicine prescriptions.
ULT stopped during the flare → record and teach that ULT continues.
GPs do not act on the plan → put a clear action and date in the summary.
Few cases → extend the window or add orthopaedic and surgical wards.
pearls: Recruit a rheumatology registrar as co-lead.
Use the pharmacy system to find colchicine starts.
Suggest a nurse-led gout clinic referral where available.
Report readmissions with gout as a secondary outcome.

pitfalls: Follow-up takes 6 months → start cycle 1 retrospectively and accept a 3-month window in cycle 2.
Joint counts done but DAS28 not calculated → count only documented scores.
Clinic capacity limits → use nurse telephone reviews with patient-reported joint counts where validated locally.
Definition of 'monthly' varies → fix the 5-week tolerance before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the rheumatology specialist nurse team early; they will deliver the slots.
Use NEIAA data to find new active cases.
Put DAS28 in the letter header so it is easy to find.
Track time to remission as the headline outcome.

pitfalls: Microbiology phones results but notes are blank → accept a documented phone call with action.
Contaminants inflate numbers → use microbiology's significance call.
Weekend results wait until Monday → report weekday and weekend separately.
Task ignored → route it to the ward pharmacist as well.
pearls: Recruit a microbiology consultant and the antimicrobial pharmacist.
Pull report times straight from the lab system.
Present bug–drug mismatches as safety events.
Pair with an IV-to-oral switch prompt.

pitfalls: Smoking status missing → count missing status as a fail and report it separately.
Patients vaping instead → record e-cigarette use and do not fail if the patient declines NRT.
NRT prescribed but not stocked on the ward → check ward stock lists first.
Opt-out order set seen as coercive → keep a one-click decline.
pearls: Recruit the tobacco dependence (CURE-type) team; they gain referrals.
Stock combination NRT on AMU.
Tell patients about ward vaping and smoking rules at clerking.
Report self-discharge rates among smokers as an outcome.

pitfalls: Foot check documented as 'feet OK' without detail → require a risk category.
Monofilaments not available → check ward stock before cycle 1.
Nurses and doctors each assume the other did it → name the nursing admission assessment as the place.
Gains fade as staff rotate → add the item to the nursing admission audit run monthly.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes inpatient specialist nurse and a podiatrist.
Keep monofilaments on each ward's observation trolley.
Link 'moderate/high risk' to automatic heel offloading and podiatry referral.
Report hospital-acquired foot lesions as the outcome that managers watch.

pitfalls: DKA episodes are few → use a 12-month window and prospective capture.
Pump users counted wrongly → exclude or record separately.
Basal dose prescribed but omitted by nursing → record administration, not just prescription.
ED starts DKA before the ward → check ED drug charts too.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes inpatient specialist nurse; they see every DKA.
Put the basal line at the top of the DKA order set.
Report rebound ketosis or readmission as outcomes.
Add a 'basal insulin given?' question to the DKA nursing care plan.

pitfalls: Meters not networked → use paper glucose charts and accept lower precision.
Reading repeated on another meter → search by patient, not meter.
Nurses treat but record late → allow a 5-minute tolerance and state it.
Prompt ignored → pair with hypo box refresh and ward feedback.
pearls: Recruit the point-of-care testing manager; they can export meter data in minutes.
Recruit a ward nurse champion on each ward.
Report recurrent hypos within 24 hours as the outcome.
Share weekly ward-level recheck rates on the diabetes dashboard.

pitfalls: Once-daily morning steroid peaks late → check that the afternoon/evening readings are included.
Meter data not linked to patients → use paper charts for cycle 1.
Short courses (<3 days) → audit days on steroid only.
Pop-up fatigue → make it a monitoring order, not an alert.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes specialist nurse and the e-prescribing pharmacist.
Use the COPD and oncology wards, where volume is high.
Teach the 'afternoon peak' in one slide.
Report hyperglycaemia >12 mmol/L days as the outcome.

pitfalls: Readings spread across blood gases and meters → search both sources.
Patients move from ED to AMU mid-monitoring → follow the patient, not the ward.
Strict time windows fail good care → state the ±15 minute tolerance before cycle 1.
Order set used but tasks not done → record completed readings, not scheduled ones.
pearls: Recruit the renal pharmacist and an ED nurse lead.
Put a printed timer card in the hyperkalaemia treatment pack.
Report hypoglycaemia rates to motivate staff.
Align with the local hyperkalaemia guideline so there is one document.

pitfalls: Patients referred straight from GP never pass through ED → limit the sample to ED/AMU referrals and state it.
'Prescribed' confused with 'given' → count only a signed administration entry.
Patients already on aspirin 75 mg are marked as passes → agree before cycle 1 that a 300 mg loading dose is still expected unless the specialist says otherwise.
Stroke mimic diagnosed later → keep them in; the standard applies to suspected TIA.
pearls: Recruit the TIA clinic nurse; they already see every referral and can flag missing doses daily.
Agree the 4-hour window with the stroke lead before cycle 1 and keep it fixed.
Ask the EPR team for a report of TIA referrals with aspirin administration times to cut collection time.
Put the result on the ED safety huddle board for a month after the change.

pitfalls: ED doctors worry about missing a bleed → agree the list of valid alternative diagnoses with the stroke lead and radiology before cycle 1.
Vague request text ('?CVA') counted as justified → define in advance that a named alternative diagnosis is required.
Radiologists vet differently between cycles → keep the same vetting rules across both cycles.
Posters alone fade → rely on the ordering-system field.
pearls: Recruit a radiology registrar; they can pull request text from RIS in one search.
Report the number of avoidable scans and radiation dose saved; managers respond to this.
Pair the change with fast-track MRI after clinic so staff feel imaging is not being withheld.
Add the rule to the junior doctor induction handbook for the next rotation.

pitfalls: Very small numbers → use a 24-month look-back and present counts, not percentages alone.
PCC given but not recorded in EPMA → cross-check the blood bank issue log.
Haematology and ED disagree on PCC dose → agree the dosing chart with haematology before the change.
Patients moved to a neurosurgical centre → collect data from the transfer letter and the receiving hospital.
pearls: Ask the transfusion practitioner to join; they own the PCC issue log.
Agree the 90-minute local timing standard with the stroke lead before cycle 1.
Add the reversal pack check to the monthly ED resus trolley checklist.
Extend to DOAC reversal once the warfarin loop is closed.

pitfalls: Observations recorded hourly, not every 15 minutes → use the bespoke chart and accept only timed readings.
Eligibility argued case by case → agree the exclusion list (NICE rec 1.5.7) with the stroke consultant before cycle 1.
Small monthly numbers → use a 12-month look-back and report counts.
Nurses unsure about infusion titration → add a titration table to the chart, reviewed by pharmacy.
pearls: Recruit a stroke specialist nurse to keep the chart stocked in ED resus.
Use SSNAP's onset and arrival times so both cycles use identical definitions.
Report both efficacy (target) and safety (drop) so critics of over-treatment are reassured.
Hand over the chart and a named owner to the next registrar at rotation.

pitfalls: Oxygen given by paramedics continues by habit → record the start time and whether hospital staff reviewed it.
Pulse oximeter over-reads in dark skin (NICE note) → collect ethnicity where recorded and discuss with the team.
Unrecorded oxygen use → check both the observation chart and the prescription.
Staff fear under-treating → share the NICE wording at the start.
pearls: Recruit a stroke nurse champion for the daily check.
Agree the handling of chronic lung disease targets before cycle 1.
Use the electronic observation system report to pull all oxygen flags in minutes.
Link the result to aspiration pneumonia and mobility, which the team already cares about.

pitfalls: Non-diabetic patients have too few readings to judge → record the number of readings and report patients with fewer than 3 separately.
Point-of-care readings not linked to EPR → ask the POCT lead for a download.
Diabetes team pushback on insulin workload → agree the correction plan with them before the change.
Hypoglycaemia from over-correction → count readings below 4 as fails.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes inpatient specialist nurse early.
Fix the 72-hour window and 1-hour action rule before cycle 1.
Use the POCT system to identify out-of-range values quickly.
Keep a named nurse owner of the protocol on the stroke unit.

pitfalls: Patients who pass a modified-texture diet are counted → define 'unable to take adequate nutrition' before cycle 1.
Families decline tubes → count a documented decision as a pass.
Out-of-hours staff unable to place tubes → collect time of day and report weekend and night delays separately.
NG tube safety never events → never shortcut position checks to meet the target.
pearls: Recruit the stroke dietitian and a nurse trained in NG placement.
Record weekend versus weekday separately; it usually explains most delays.
Add 'NG decision' as a fixed line on the stroke board round.
Share results with the nutrition steering group to keep support after rotation.

pitfalls: Statins held deliberately for haemorrhage → count a documented reason as a pass.
Omission codes misused → cross-check with notes for 5 random cases.
Confusion with rec 1.4.21 (no immediate new start) → the audit covers only patients already on a statin.
Pharmacy reconciliation delayed → use the GP record where reconciliation is missing.
pearls: Partner with the stroke ward pharmacist; they already review omissions.
Use the EPMA omitted-dose report to cut collection time.
Agree the handling of intensity changes (for example switch to atorvastatin 80 mg) before cycle 1.
Include the result in the monthly medicines safety report so it survives rotation.

pitfalls: Coding misses seizures recorded as 'collapse' → search both codes and screen notes.
Neurology capacity is the real barrier → present the gap as slots needed per week, not blame.
Patients referred to GP instead → count as not referred.
Changing the definition of first seizure between cycles → fix the exclusion list before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit a neurologist or epilepsy nurse who runs the clinic.
Count slots needed per week from cycle 1 data and ask for exactly that.
Add DVLA advice as a second field; it is often missing and easy to fix together.
Make the ED discharge letter auto-copy the first-seizure clinic.

pitfalls: ECG done but not reviewed → require a documented interpretation.
ECG stored only on paper → check the ECG system and scanned notes.
Triage nurses overloaded → agree with the nurse lead before adding to triage.
Small numbers of abnormal ECGs → report them as cases, not rates.
pearls: Recruit the ED triage nurse lead.
Pull the ECG system's timestamp list to save time.
Combine with the first-seizure referral audit for one data collection.
Add the triage order set to the ED induction slides.

pitfalls: 'Typical' not documented → treat missing as not typical and report separately.
Head injury during seizure is common → use NICE head injury criteria as the agreed 'other concern'.
Radiology vetting changes between cycles → keep the same vetting rules.
Fear of litigation → present the zero-miss results from cycle 1 CT findings.
pearls: Recruit the ED consultant who leads imaging governance.
Show the number of new findings in cycle 1; usually near zero.
Pair with an ED seizure proforma that records 'typical: yes/no'.
Keep a named radiology link for the second cycle.

pitfalls: Discussion held but not written → the template line fixes documentation, not only practice.
Clinicians worry about distressing patients → share the NICE rationale and patient charity leaflets.
Letters from other hospitals not visible → use only local letters and state this.
Definition drift between cycles → fix the 12-month look-back.
pearls: Recruit an epilepsy specialist nurse as co-lead.
Include a SUDEP leaflet link in the template.
Agree the template wording with all consultants before cycle 1.
Report by clinician privately to encourage uptake.

pitfalls: Coding misses status recorded as 'seizure' → also screen admissions with IV lorazepam given.
'Concern of recurrence' judged differently → agree the definition with neurology before cycle 1.
Epilepsy nurse capacity → estimate yearly numbers from cycle 1.
Plans written but not shared with carers → collect carer training as a separate field.
pearls: Recruit the epilepsy nurse team as owners.
Use the pharmacy dispensing log for buccal midazolam to find cases.
Store the plan template on the intranet next to the discharge letter template.
Present to acute medicine, where most patients are discharged from.

pitfalls: Discussion done but not recorded → the template line fixes this.
Letters written by different clinicians use different headings → agree the template with all clinicians.
Levodopa-only patients also at risk → optional second cohort, but keep cycle 1 and 2 identical.
Patients embarrassed → include carer questioning as a separate field.
pearls: Recruit the Parkinson's specialist nurse.
Use the QUIP short questionnaire if clinicians want a tool, but only the discussion is audited.
Link to NICE rec 1.4.3 (information at start of agonist) for a second cycle.
Share a one-line script for asking about gambling, shopping, eating and sex.

pitfalls: Prescribing from order sets (for example post-operative nausea) → review antiemetic order sets too.
Metoclopramide not named in the NICE wording → audit it as a separate field.
Alert fatigue → restrict the alert to the patients with Parkinson's drugs on the chart.
Delirium pathways recommend haloperidol → update the delirium guideline at the same time.
pearls: Recruit an EPMA pharmacist to build the report and the alert.
Offer domperidone and ondansetron alternatives in the alert text.
Involve the Parkinson's nurse in the governance paper.
Re-run the EPMA report quarterly to keep gains.

pitfalls: Delirium present but never named in notes → include only patients with a documented diagnosis or positive 4AT.
Field ticked 'no' by default → make it an active choice without a default.
GPs may not read the field → ask one local GP to review sample summaries.
Short-stay patients discharged by juniors unaware → include the field in the discharge checklist.
pearls: Recruit a frailty consultant and the clinical coding lead.
Show the coding income gain; managers often support it.
Add a single-line leaflet for families about delirium to the discharge pack.
Assign a named ward registrar to check the field weekly for 2 months.

pitfalls: Emergency doses given at night before an ECG is possible → allow a 24-hour catch-up with a documented reason.
Haloperidol used as antiemetic confuses the sample → filter by indication in notes.
ECG done but QTc not read → require the QTc value.
Pushback about delaying treatment → stress non-drug measures come first (NICE CG103 rec 1.7.3).
pearls: Recruit an EPMA pharmacist and a frailty consultant.
Also record Parkinson's or Lewy body disease; any use there is a separate safety finding.
Use the ECG system to confirm times, not the notes.
Present the result alongside the NICE delirium pathway to keep it in context.

pitfalls: Score calculated but no action → audit the decision step as part of the pass.
Different ACB scales between cycles → fix one scale before cycle 1.
Psychiatric drugs started by others → document 'continue with reason' as a valid decision.
Short stays → limit to stays of 72 hours or more.
pearls: Recruit the ward pharmacist as co-lead.
Print the top 10 local anticholinergic drugs with alternatives on the ward round sheet.
Send the score to the GP in the discharge summary so the change lasts.
Keep the report in the monthly pharmacy dashboard.

pitfalls: Night-time PRN doses become regular without discussion → count the first regular dose as the trigger.
Family unreachable → accept a documented attempt with time and number called.
Psychiatry liaison starts drug → the standard still applies; include them in the change.
Checklist ticked without discussion → spot-check 5 notes for a free-text record.
pearls: Recruit the dementia lead nurse and liaison psychiatry.
Print the NICE patient decision aid for ward packs.
Agree what counts as 'regular' with pharmacy before cycle 1.
Report antipsychotics continued at discharge as a secondary outcome for GPs.

pitfalls: Fall time missing on incident report → use the nursing entry time and flag it.
Reviews not documented at night → record night falls separately.
Incident system under-reports falls → cross-check with ward safety huddle records.
Doctors see it as extra work → keep the form short (6 fields).
pearls: Recruit the falls prevention nurse and ward sisters.
Use the incident system as the sampling frame so both cycles match.
Report the 30-minute injury subgroup separately (NAIF measure).
Include the form in junior doctor induction and bleep holder handbook.

pitfalls: 'Medications reviewed' written without detail → require a decision per FRID.
Disagreement on the FRID list → adopt a published list (for example STOPPFall) before cycle 1.
Pharmacist capacity → prioritise patients with 3 or more FRIDs.
Changes not passed to GP → include 'changes in discharge summary' as a field.
pearls: Recruit the ward pharmacist as co-lead.
Print the FRID list on the post-fall form.
Combine data collection with the 12-hour medical examination audit.
Report the number of FRIDs stopped; it motivates teams.

pitfalls: Start date unknown → use GP record; exclude if still unknown.
High-risk patients (previous vertebral fracture) should continue → a documented 'continue' decision is a pass.
Clinicians think it is the GP's job → present it as a shared review, copied to the GP.
Numbers too low in one clinic → include ward discharges.
pearls: Recruit the fracture liaison nurse.
Provide a one-line FRAX link in the template.
Agree with local GPs who owns the decision after the letter.
Add the template line permanently so it survives rotation.

pitfalls: Recognition of dying time unclear → use the first documented statement that the person is dying.
Order sets used blindly → keep 'individualise and review daily' wording and a palliative contact.
Palliative team concern about standardisation → co-design the order set with them.
Deaths spread over many wards → sample through the bereavement office list, not wards.
pearls: Recruit the hospital palliative care nurse specialist and an EPMA pharmacist.
Link the audit to NACEL so the trust already has a governance route.
Include renal dosing; it is the most common error.
Add the order set to the end-of-life care plan document.

pitfalls: Nursing and medical notes in different systems → check both.
'Comfortable' entries counted as assessment → define what counts before cycle 1.
Families distressed by 'withholding fluids' → pair with the discussion field and leaflet.
Deaths with short dying phase → require 48 hours so every day can be judged.
pearls: Recruit the palliative care nurse specialist and ward matrons.
Use NACEL case note review forms to align definitions.
Keep the care plan box short (three lines).
Share one anonymised good example at ward huddles.

pitfalls: As-required laxatives counted → count only regular prescriptions.
Weak opioids (codeine) included by mistake → list strong opioids before cycle 1.
Alert fatigue → only trigger the prompt when no regular laxative is on the chart.
Patients refuse laxatives → still a pass if prescribed; record refusals.
pearls: Recruit the ward pharmacist; the EPMA report takes minutes.
Suggest a default stimulant laxative in the order set.
Record bowel outcome as a balancing measure.
Share results with surgery too; the same EPMA change helps them.

pitfalls: Disagreement on what is 'non-symptomatic' → agree a list with palliative care before cycle 1.
Anticoagulants for AF debated → count a documented reason as a pass.
Families want medicines continued → the discussion field captures this.
Recognition of dying reversed → exclude patients who stabilised and were discharged.
pearls: Recruit the palliative care consultant and ward pharmacist.
Run the EPMA 'active prescriptions' report at recognition time for quick data.
Count doses given after recognition; it is a striking figure.
Pair with the anticipatory medicines audit to share data collection.

pitfalls: Out-of-hours assessors cannot print in the emergency department → allow a copy by text or email, or a handwritten crisis card, to count as a pass.
Notes say 'plan discussed' but not 'copy given' → define the pass wording before cycle 1 and keep it the same in cycle 2.
People who leave soon after assessment skew the rate → record 'left before copy could be given' separately.
Staff see the tick box as more paperwork → show them the NG225 wording and keep the box to one click.
pearls: Recruit the liaison team manager and one band 6 nurse as co-leads; they own the template.
Agree with IT a one-page printable plan built from fields already in the assessment.
Keep a stock of printed crisis cards in the emergency department mental health room.
Hand the monthly count to the team manager so it survives the trainee rotation.

pitfalls: Some staff and commissioners still expect a risk grade → agree with the clinical director before cycle 1 that the grade is being removed on NG225 grounds.
Recording a grade is not a fail if it is not the reason → audit the reason, not the presence of the word.
The drop-down is part of a trust-wide form → pilot a liaison-only version first.
Judging 'needs-based' is subjective → two auditors score the first 10 cases and agree the rule.
pearls: Bring the trust suicide prevention lead on side; they usually want this change.
Use real anonymised notes to show the difference between a grade and a formulation.
Pair the template change with the safety plan audit so the box is not left empty.
Ask the governance team to keep the monthly score after the audit team moves on.

pitfalls: Debriefs happen but are not written down → count only what is documented and say so when presenting.
Staff debrief is confused with patient debrief → keep them as separate fields.
Patients who remain very unwell for days → allow 'deferred, reason recorded' but report it separately.
Ward staff feel judged → frame it as a patient-experience measure and share results by ward, not by name.
pearls: Recruit a ward manager, the restrictive practice lead and a peer support worker.
Ask advocacy services to accept debrief referrals directly.
Put the debrief prompt on the safety huddle board for patients restrained in the last 72 hours.
The incident form field keeps the change after the audit team rotates.

pitfalls: Paper rights forms are filed but not scanned → agree with the Mental Health Act office to use their tracker as the source.
Repeat explanations are done but written only in nursing notes → search nursing notes as well as forms.
Small numbers on one ward → pool all adult acute wards.
Nurses see it as an administrative task → show the Code wording and the Care Quality Commission focus on rights.
pearls: The Mental Health Act administrator is the key ally; they already track rights.
Agree what 'understood' means (patient can say it back in their own words) before cycle 1.
Easy-read and translated leaflets should be at the nursing station, not in an office.
Hand the monthly report to the Mental Health Act office manager.

pitfalls: Capacity for advocacy is rarely recorded as such → accept 'did not understand rights' as the trigger and define it before cycle 1.
The advocacy provider keeps its own records → ask them for a referral list for the audit period.
Older adult and learning disability wards may have few cases → pool across wards.
Concern that opt-out referral breaches consent → the Code allows it for patients who lack capacity; confirm with the Mental Health Act lead.
pearls: Invite the advocacy service manager to the planning meeting; they often want this data.
Use the Mental Health Act office as the single point that sends referrals.
Include older adult wards, where lack of capacity is most common.
Add the referral date to the rights tracker so it is checked every month.

pitfalls: Copies are given but not recorded → the new box makes it visible; do not count cycle 1 as bad practice without explanation.
Forms are scanned late → check the ward folder as well as the electronic record.
Responsible clinicians change forms often → count each new authorisation as one case.
Staff worry patients will lose the form → offer a copy kept in the patient's room or locker.
pearls: Recruit the Mental Health Act administrator and one ward manager.
Agree that 'offered and declined' counts as a pass.
Ask responsible clinicians to hand the form to the named nurse straight after the ward round.
Add the item to the existing Mental Health Act office spot checks.

pitfalls: The AMHP service is run by the local authority → involve the AMHP lead from the start; they own half of the target.
Arrival time is recorded differently by police and staff → use the place of safety log time only.
Intoxicated patients inflate breaches → record the clinical reason and report both rates.
Staffing shortages at night → split results by in-hours and out-of-hours to target the fix.
pearls: Get the s136 multi-agency meeting to sign off the audit in advance.
Record the reason for each breach using fixed codes.
Keep the escalation rule simple: 2 hours without a doctor or AMHP means a call to the consultant.
Hand the monthly rate to the place of safety manager.

pitfalls: Defining 'adequate trial' is contentious → agree dose and duration with the lead consultant before cycle 1.
Old records are incomplete → accept clinic letters as evidence of past trials.
Consultants may feel criticised → present as a caseload opportunity, not individual failure.
Offers are made verbally and not written → the template line makes it visible.
pearls: Recruit the clozapine clinic pharmacist; they can search dispensing records quickly.
Share a patient leaflet on clozapine to support the discussion.
Present anonymised examples of people who waited years for clozapine.
Ask the pharmacy team to run the caseload search yearly after the audit.
